blocks.heading: Cornell Universal Front
rows: How did federal land and railroad policy reshape the West — and at whose expense?
Homestead Act · Transcontinental Railroad · Manifest Destiny · Promontory Summit
I can sequence westward expansion and weigh who benefited and who bore the cost.

head: Term
What it means
Español
rows: An 1862 law that provided 160 acres of public land to settlers who agreed to live on. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.
A continuous railroad line completed in 1869 that connected the eastern United States with the Pacific coast. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.
The 19th-century movement of settlers, railroads, and U.S. authority across the continent toward the Pacific, encouraged by free land and new transportation.
The widely held 1800s belief that the United States was destined to expand across the entire continent, used to justify the displacement of American Indians.
A gift of public land from the government — to railroad companies or settlers — used to fund and accelerate western settlement.
An area of land set aside by the federal government for American Indian tribes, frequently far from their ancestral homelands.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.03 (synthesize) and SSP.05 (historical awareness).

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Sequence the expansion of the United States. The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of free land to settlers who would farm it for five years. Combined with the completion of the Transcontinental Railroad in 1869, these policies accelerated westward expansion as part of Manifest Destiny—the belief that Americans were destined to spread across the continent. The Union Pacific built westward from Omaha while the Central Pacific built eastward from Sacramento, meeting at Promontory Summit, Utah.

Impact on Western Settlement. The Transcontinental Railroad dramatically reduced travel time from months to days, opening the West to settlement, commerce, and resource extraction. Towns sprang up along rail lines, and agricultural products could reach eastern markets efficiently — but this expansion came at tremendous cost to American Indian nations whose lands were taken and whose way of life was destroyed.

Impact on American Indians, Immigrants, and Settlers. Western expansion devastated American Indian communities through forced relocations, broken treaties, and the near-extinction of the buffalo herds they depended upon. Chinese workers who built much of the Central Pacific faced discrimination despite their crucial contributions. The “Buffalo Soldiers”—African American cavalry regiments—served on the frontier, including George Jordan of Williamson County, Tennessee, who earned the Medal of Honor.

blocks.heading: Cornell Universal Front
rows: How did federal policy try to erase Native nations — and how did they resist?
Teacher & Student decks — US.02 section (advance in order)
Reservation System · Assimilation · Dawes Act · Allotment · Boarding School
I can examine federal policies toward American Indians, including the movement to reservations, assimilation, boarding schools, and the Dawes Act.

head: Term
What it means
Español
rows: Federal policy that confined Native American tribes to designated areas of land. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.
Federal policy aimed at forcing Native Americans to abandon their traditional cultures and adopt European-American ways of life. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.
An 1887 law that divided tribal lands into individual allotments for Native American families. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.
The division of communal tribal land into small individual plots under the Dawes Act, which opened "surplus" land to white settlers and caused massive Native land loss.
Off-reservation schools, such as Carlisle, where Native children were forced to abandon their languages, names, and cultures to be "assimilated" into white society.
The right of a tribe or nation to govern itself; federal Indian policy in this era steadily eroded tribal sovereignty.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.01, SSP.02, SSP.03 — collect, examine, and synthesize evidence with historical awareness.

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Movement to Reservations. After the Civil War, the federal government expanded a policy of confining American Indian nations to reservations—designated territories far smaller than their traditional homelands. Officials stated two goals: to open western land for white settlement and railroads, and to end armed conflict on the Plains. Many treaties were signed under military and economic pressure, and tribes surrendered millions of acres. Resistance continued: at the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876), Lakota and Cheyenne forces under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Lt. Col. George Custer—a Native victory that intensified U.S. efforts to break tribal power.

Assimilation and Boarding Schools. Alongside removal, the government pursued a policy of assimilation—using schools and law to replace tribal cultures with Euro-American ones. At off-reservation boarding schools such as the Carlisle Indian Industrial School (founded 1879), Captain Richard H. Pratt summarized the aim in 1892: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.” Children were removed from their families and often forbidden to speak their languages, wear their clothing, or practice their religions. Historians today describe this systematic effort to erase Native identity as cultural genocide, and document its lasting, multi-generational harm.

The Dawes Act and Its Impact. The Dawes Severalty Act of 1887 broke up communal tribal lands into individual allotments—160 acres to each head of a family—stating the goal of turning American Indians into independent farmers and U.S. citizens. The actual effect was a massive transfer of land: American Indians held about 150 million acres before the Act, and lost roughly two-thirds of their land base—over 90 million acres—by 1934. “Surplus” land was sold to white settlers, and additional allotted land was lost through taxation, fraud, and forced sales. The Act dismantled the communal landholding central to many tribal cultures.

standards.title: Compromise of 1877, Jim Crow & Plessy v. Ferguson

blocks.heading: Cornell Universal Front
rows: How did the end of Reconstruction harden into Jim Crow — and who fought back?
Teacher & Student decks — US.03 section (advance in order)
Compromise of 1877 · Jim Crow Laws · Disenfranchisement · Plessy v. Ferguson · Exodusters

I can explain the impact of the Compromise of 1877, including Jim Crow laws, lynching, disenfranchisement methods, the efforts of Benjamin "Pap" Singleton and the Exodusters, and the Plessy v. Ferguson decision.

head: Term
What it means
Español
rows: An informal agreement that resolved the disputed 1876 presidential election. It changed who held power after major conflicts.
State and local laws enacted primarily in the Southern states between 1877 and the 1960s that enforced racial. It shaped racial rules and unequal treatment in daily life.
The systematic taking away of voting rights through methods such as poll taxes. It changed who could vote and who had political power.
An 1896 Supreme Court decision that upheld racial separation by race under the doctrine of "separate but equal,". It shaped racial rules and unequal treatment in daily life.
African Americans who moved from the South to Kansas and other western states in the late 1870s. It shaped racial rules and unequal treatment in daily life.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.01, SSP.02, SSP.03 — collect, examine, and synthesize evidence with historical awareness.

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: The Election of 1876 and End of Reconstruction. The disputed 1876 presidential election between Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel Tilden led to the Compromise of 1877. In exchange for the presidency, Hayes agreed to withdraw federal troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction. This abandonment left African Americans without federal protection against increasingly hostile state governments.

Jim Crow Laws, Lynching, and Disenfranchisement. With federal protection gone, Southern states implemented Jim Crow laws enforcing racial segregation in all aspects of life. African Americans faced systematic disenfranchisement through poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and white primaries. Those who resisted faced terrorism, including lynching—public murders that went unpunished and were often celebrated by white communities.

Pap Singleton and the Exodusters. Benjamin "Pap" Singleton, a formerly enslaved man, organized the migration of thousands of African Americans from the South to Kansas in 1879. These "Exodusters" sought to escape violence and oppression, establishing communities like Nicodemus, Kansas. While conditions in Kansas were often harsh, the Exoduster movement represented African American agency and resistance to Jim Crow terror.

Plessy v. Ferguson and "Separate But Equal". The 1896 Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson established the "separate but equal" doctrine, ruling that racial segregation was constitutional as long as facilities were supposedly equal. In practice, facilities for African Americans were grossly inferior. This decision legitimized Jim Crow segregation for nearly sixty years until Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

blocks.heading: Cornell Universal Front

Teacher & Student decks — US.04 section (advance in order)
Gilded Age · Political Machines · Spoils System · Boss Tweed · Thomas Nast

I can analyze the causes and consequences of Gilded Age politics and economics, including political machines, major scandals, civil service reform, and economic differences between farmers, wage earners, and industrial capitalists.

head: Term
What it means
Español
rows: The period from roughly 1870 to 1900 characterized by rapid economic growth. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.
Corrupt organizations that controlled city politics through patronage. It changed who could vote and who had political power.
The practice of rewarding political supporters with government jobs regardless of qualifications. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.
He led New York City's Tammany Hall machine and used bribery to control city politics. His group stole millions of dollars from taxpayers through corrupt contracts.
A political cartoonist whose illustrations exposed Boss Tweed's corruption and helped bring down the Tammany Hall machine. It changed daily life, rights, or power during this era.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.01, SSP.02, SSP.03 — collect, examine, and synthesize evidence with historical awareness.

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Political Machines and Boss Tweed. The Gilded Age (1870s-1900) saw the rise of powerful political machines that controlled city governments through patronage and corruption. Boss Tweed's Tammany Hall in New York City epitomized this system, funneling millions in public funds to Tweed and his associates. Political cartoonist Thomas Nast exposed Tweed's corruption through devastating illustrations in Harper's Weekly.

Major Scandals and the Spoils System. The era was marked by corruption at all levels. The Crédit Mobilier scandal revealed that railroad executives and congressmen had profited enormously from fraudulent construction contracts. The spoils system—giving government jobs to political supporters regardless of qualification—reached its peak. President James Garfield's assassination by a disappointed office-seeker in 1881 finally prompted reform.

Civil Service Reform. Garfield's assassination led to the Pendleton Civil Service Act of 1883, which established merit-based hiring for federal positions through competitive examinations. This began the long process of professionalizing government service, though political influence remained significant in many positions.

Economic Disparity. The Gilded Age saw extreme wealth concentration among industrial capitalists while farmers struggled with falling crop prices, high railroad shipping rates, and debt. Wage earners faced dangerous working conditions, long hours, and low pay. The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 attempted to regulate railroad rates, representing early federal intervention in the economy.

blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.01, SSP.02, SSP.05 — collect, examine, and synthesize evidence with historical awareness.

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Technological Innovations. The late 19th century saw transformative inventions that reshaped American life. Alexander Graham Bell's telephone (1876) revolutionized communication. Thomas Edison's electrical systems and light bulb brought power to homes and factories. Nikola Tesla's alternating current system enabled long-distance electrical transmission. Henry Bessemer's steel process made skyscrapers and modern infrastructure possible.

Industrial Titans. Andrew Carnegie built a steel empire through vertical integration, controlling every step from iron mines to finished products. John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil pioneered horizontal integration, buying out competitors to dominate the oil industry. J.P. Morgan wielded enormous financial power, reorganizing railroads and creating U.S. Steel. Cornelius Vanderbilt consolidated railroad networks, enabling national commerce.

African American Entrepreneurs. Despite facing discrimination, African American entrepreneurs made significant contributions. Madam C.J. Walker became America's first female self-made millionaire through her hair care products, employing thousands of Black women. George Washington Carver's agricultural research at Tuskegee Institute developed hundreds of products from peanuts and sweet potatoes, helping diversify Southern agriculture.

Teacher & Student decks — US.06 section (advance in order)

I can locate major industrial centers and describe how industrialization influenced the movement of people from rural to urban areas.

head: Term
What it means
Español
rows: The rapid growth of cities due to factory growth and mass moving. It changed where people lived and worked in growing cities.
A farmers' organization formed in the 1860s-1870s to combat the power of railroads and grain elevator companies. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.
A political movement representing the interests of ordinary people. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.01, SSP.05, SSP.06 — collect, examine, and synthesize evidence with historical awareness.

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Major Industrial Centers. Industrialization concentrated in cities with geographic advantages. Pittsburgh became the steel capital due to access to coal, iron ore, and rivers. Chicago emerged as a railroad hub and meatpacking center. New York City dominated finance and trade through its port. Boston led in textiles and manufacturing. San Francisco served as the gateway to Pacific trade and western resources.

Rural-to-Urban Migration. Industrialization drew millions from farms to cities seeking factory jobs. The promise of wages attracted both native-born Americans and immigrants. Cities grew explosively—Chicago's population increased from 30,000 in 1850 to over 1 million by 1890. This rapid growth created overcrowded tenements, inadequate sanitation, and new social challenges.

Geographic Factors in Industrial Location. Industries located based on access to raw materials, transportation, markets, and labor. Steel mills clustered near coal and iron deposits. Textile mills used water power and later concentrated near ports for cotton imports. Meatpacking centered in Chicago due to railroad connections to cattle ranges and eastern markets. These patterns shaped regional development for generations.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.01, SSP.02, SSP.03 — collect, examine, and synthesize evidence with historical awareness.

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Old and New Immigrants. "Old" immigrants (pre-1880) came primarily from Northern and Western Europe—Britain, Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia. They often spoke English or related languages and were predominantly Protestant. "New" immigrants (1880-1920) came from Southern and Eastern Europe—Italy, Poland, Russia, Greece—as well as Asia. They brought different languages, religions (Catholic, Orthodox, Jewish), and customs that many Americans viewed with suspicion.

Entry Points and the Assimilation Process. Ellis Island in New York Harbor processed millions of European immigrants, while Angel Island in San Francisco served Asian immigrants with far more restrictive procedures. New immigrants faced difficult assimilation: language barriers, discrimination, and unfamiliar customs. Jane Addams's Hull House in Chicago pioneered settlement houses that helped immigrants learn English, navigate American systems, and maintain cultural connections.

Push and Pull Factors. Push factors drove people from their homelands: religious persecution (especially of Jews in Russia), poverty, political upheaval, and lack of opportunity. Pull factors attracted them to America: economic opportunity, religious freedom, land availability, and established immigrant communities. Letters from successful immigrants encouraged others to follow.

Nativism and Restriction. The rise of nativism—hostility toward immigrants—led to restrictive legislation. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 banned Chinese immigration for ten years (repeatedly renewed until 1943). The Gentleman's Agreement of 1907 limited Japanese immigration. Jacob Riis's photographs and writings, including "How the Other Half Lives," exposed immigrant living conditions, prompting both sympathy and nativist fears.

blocks.name: Primary Source (HIPPO)
blocks.lead: Analyze a verified primary source with HIPPO: Historical context, Intended audience, Point of view, Purpose, Outside evidence. Builds SSP.01–SSP.02.

blocks.label: Source it first
paras: Every source gets sourced before it gets analyzed. Fill the HIPPO frame, then answer the guiding question in a complete CER (Claim – Evidence – Reasoning).

head: HIPPO move
What I notice in this source
rows: Historical context — what was happening when this was made?
Intended audience — who was meant to see it?
Point of view — whose perspective, and what is left out?
Outside evidence — what do I already know that connects?

blocks.name: Two Sides of Immigration
blocks.lead: Use evidence from the reading and the source to build your answer.

blocks.label: Task — Pairs → Whole class · 12 min
paras: Examine Jacob Riis's “Five Cents a Spot” photograph and the Ellis Island inspection-room image. Write one sentence from the perspective of a new immigrant and one from a nativist worried about change. Then explain what Riis wanted viewers to FEEL and DO.
Deliverable: Two perspective sentences + a photographer's-purpose statement.

blocks.label: Differentiation
paras: Entry: sentence stems for both perspectives. Honors: evaluate whether a staged photo is reliable evidence.

blocks.heading: Cornell Notes (25 / 75)
cues: Who benefited? Who bore the cost?
